articles.title: Ranking Every Player in Rays vs. Brewers 2026 World Series Matchup From 52 to 1
articles.summary: The 2026 World Series begins on Friday night, and while the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays matchup doesn't have the same level of name recognition we've seen the past few years in the Fall Classic, there is no shortage of star power.
articles.body:
The 2026 World Series begins on Friday night, and while the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays matchup doesn't have the same level of name recognition we've seen the past few years in the Fall Classic, there is no shortage of star power.

Milwaukee ace Jacob Misiorowski and Tampa Bay slugger Junior Caminero are the most recognizable names set to take the field, but both rosters feature electric arms and well-constructed lineups that can put runs on the board in a variety of different ways.

Ahead of the first pitch in Game 1, we've ranked all 52 players set to take the field in the 2026 World Series.

Players are ranked based on their 2026 production, importance to their team and more recent performance during the postseason. This is not meant to be a rundown of career accomplishments. It's a preview of who is most likely to make an impact on baseball's biggest stage in the coming days.

52-42 | 41-36 | 35-30 | 29-25 | 24-20 | 19-15 | 14-12 | 11-9 | 8-6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1

Long relievers Brody Hopkins, Kyle Harrison and Chad Patrick have yet to make an appearance this postseason, while Cole Sulser (0.2 IP, 3 ER), Shane Drohan (1.0 IP, 1 ER), Steven Matz (2.0 IP, 0 ER) and Antonio Senzatela (1.2 IP, 0 ER) have been used sparingly.

Never say never when it comes to arms being needed in the World Series—just ask Will Klein. However, no one from that group of arms is expected to log key innings in the World Series.

Cedric Mullins, Nick Fortes and Jorge Mateo have a combined seven plate appearances for the Rays in the playoffs, while Gary Sánchez walked in his lone trip to the plate. Mullins does have a home run and a steal, so he's one to keep an eye on for a potential late-inning impact.

41. OF Luis Lara, MIL 40. IF Ben Williamson, TB 39. OF Ryan Vilade, TB 38. 3B Joey Ortiz, MIL 37. DH Andrew Vaughn, MIL

Both teams utilize platoons at multiple positions.

For Milwaukee, Luis Lara, Joey Ortiz and Andrew Vaughn generally start in place of Sal Frelick (RF), David Hamilton (3B) and Christian Yelich (DH) when a left-handed starter is on the mound. The Rays don't have a lefty starter with Shane McClanahan injured, but Vaughn could see some pinch-hit opportunities against Ian Seymour or Cam Booser.

On the other side, Ben Williamson and Ryan Vilade have spelled Richie Palacios (2B) and Victor Mesa Jr. (RF) against southpaws, and that will be relevant when Robert Gasser toes the rubber for Milwaukee. Vilade had an .818 OPS and seven home runs in 170 plate appearances against lefties during the regular season.

May had a 4.38 ERA in 109 innings with the Cardinals before he was traded to the Brewers at the deadline along with reliever JoJo Romero, but he struggled to a 5.65 ERA following the trade and has allowed five earned runs in seven innings this postseason. He will be a candidate to start Game 4 along with Shane Drohan, though a couple innings in a bullpen game is more likely.

35. RHP Tyler Wells, TB 34. LHP Ian Seymour, TB

Wells was fantastic after he was acquired from the Orioles at the trade deadline, but he has allowed multiple runs in two of his four appearances this postseason and fallen down the bullpen pecking order.

Seymour has chewed up 7.1 innings over six appearances this postseason. He slots in as the second lefty behind Cam Booser, but his work will likely be limited to multi-inning bulk work.

33. OF Sal Frelick, MIL 32. DH Christian Yelich, MIL 31. 2B Richie Palacios, TB 30. 3B David Hamilton, MIL

These players represent the strong side of the platoons mentioned on the previous slide, and while Frelick (3-for-15) is having a quiet postseason, Hamilton (5-for-11, HR) and Yelich (7-for-24) have both been productive.

Palacios (8-for-22, 3 2B) has also provided a nice spark at the bottom of the Tampa Bay lineup, and he adds secondary value with his glove and his legs.

29. LHP JoJo Romero, MIL 28. RHP Kevin Kelly, TB 27. LHP Cam Booser, TB

Romero has struck out nine of the 19 batters he has faced this postseason while allowing just one earned run, and his ability to work high-leverage spots gives Milwaukee more flexibility in how they deploy fellow lefties Aaron Ashby and DL Hall.

Kevin Kelly and Cam Booser each have four holds and serve as the primary late-inning setup bridge to closer Bryan Baker, with Booser in particular having a standout postseason with 4.2 scoreless innings over six appearances.

DeLuca hit .276/.306/.432 after the All-Star break while settling in as an everyday starter, and that offensive production is a bonus on top of his strong defensive game (4 DRS, 6 OAA) in center field. The 28-year-old is 6-for-30 with a double and two steals in the playoffs.

Jax posted a 3.53 ERA, 1.18 WHIP and 116 strikeouts in 112.1 innings spanning 23 starts and 11 relief appearances, making a smooth transition into a starting role. He took the loss in Game 3 of the ALCS (4.0 IP, 5 H, 3 ER, 2 BB, 2 K), and while he is the leading candidate for a Game 4 start, he could also make an impact out of the bullpen.

24. SS Cooper Pratt, MIL 23. SS Taylor Walls, TB

Pratt (9-for-29, .655 OPS) and Walls (4-for-27, .381 OPS) both provide limited offensive impact and standout defense at a premium position. They hit a combined five home runs in 699 plate appearances during the regular season and a double in Game 4 of the NLDS by Pratt is their lone extra-base hit, but their glove work still makes them key pieces of the World Series puzzle.

Hall has high-octane stuff from the left side and has been one of Milwaukee's most reliable late-inning arms all season. He had a 1.91 ERA and 9.4 K/9 in 61.1 innings during the regular season, and has tossed 5.1 scoreless innings so far this postseason. Walks can be an issue at times, but he has been lights out.

21. OF Victor Mesa Jr., TB 20. C Liam Hicks, TB

The Rays had a top-heavy lineup for much of the first half of the season with Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda doing most of the heavy lifting offensively.

The addition of Hicks at the deadline and emergence of Mesa as the primary right fielder added some much-needed length to their lineup, and while both have been relatively quiet so far this postseason, they are capable of making a significant impact.

Armed with a fastball that averages 98.8 mph and a slider that is generating a 38.0 percent whiff rate, Uribe has closer-caliber stuff serving as Milwaukee's primary setup man.

He allowed just five hits and one unearned run in his first six appearances this postseason before a shaky outing in Game 4 of the NLCS (0.1 IP, 1 H, 3 BB, 2 ER), but he has been one of the game's top setup relievers the last few years.

18. OF Chandler Simpson, TB 17. 1B Jonathan Aranda, TB

Simpson has elite contact skills and electric speed, while Aranda is one of the few consistent power threats in the Tampa Bay lineup. Both have a sub-.700 OPS in the playoffs, but they were two of the club's offensive standouts during the regular season and will be counted on to make their mark on the Fall Classic.

16. RHP Logan Henderson, MIL 15. LHP Robert Gasser, MIL

Henderson did not allow more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts during the regular season. That has continued in the playoffs, as he was the Game 2 starter for both the NLDS (5.0 IP, 2 H, 1 ER) and NLCS (4.0 IP, 3 H, 4 R, 2 ER), taking a no-decision in both outings.

Gasser came on strong late with a 1.67 ERA in 32.1 innings over his final six starts, and he threw it well in Game 4 of the NLDS (4.0 IP, 3 H, 1 ER) and Game 3 of the NLCS (5.0 IP, 3 H, 0 ER). Who would have guessed he would be one of the team's top three starters just a few months ago?

The one-year, $13 million deal Martinez signed with the Rays in February turned out to be one of the best moves of the offseason. The 36-year-old was an All-Star for the first time, going 15-6 with a 3.10 ERA in a team-high 180 innings.

He was the winning pitcher in Game 4 of the ALCS (5.1 IP, 2 H, 1 ER), and while he doesn't strike out a ton of batters, he thrives on elite command and weak contact .

13. RHP Trevor Megill, MIL 12. RHP Bryan Baker, TB

Baker (65 G, 41/44 SV, 1.44 ERA, 9.1 K/9) and Megill (63 G, 30/33 SV, 2.63 ERA, 10.1 K/9) were two of the most dominant closers in baseball this season, and that has continued in October as they have nailed down all nine combined save chances.

The Brewers have sometimes relied on Aaron Ashby to get things across the finish line, so Baker gets the higher spot in the rankings simply due to his slightly elevated importance to his team's success.

11. OF Garrett Mitchell, MIL 10. OF Jackson Chourio, MIL 9. 2B Brice Turang, MIL

Turang (7.3), Chourio (4.9) and Mitchell (3.4) racked up a combined 15.6 WAR during the regular season, checking in as the top three on Milwaukee's WAR leaderboard among position players.

Chourio and Mitchell have each slugged two home runs in the playoffs, while Turang has a terrific .382 on-base percentage thanks to six hits and seven walks in eight games.

Outside of their contributions at the plate, which have been modest in October relative to their regular-season production, all three are also standout defenders. Turang and Chourio are Gold Glove finalists, while Mitchell (1,105 INN, 7 DRS, 7 OAA) has standout defensive metrics in center field.

8. 1B Jake Bauers, MIL 7. RHP Freddy Peralta, TB

The ALCS and NLCS MVP winners also have the unique distinction of facing off against the team they broke into the big leagues with in this World Series matchup.

Bauers (140 OPS+, 26 HR, 3.3 WAR) has authored one of the biggest breakouts in baseball, while Peralta (10 GS, 3.25 ERA, 55.1 IP) immediately turned around a disappointing season when he joined the Rays at the trade deadline.

Peralta had a 0.75 ERA in 12 innings in the ALCS, recording two wins and a hold in relief, while Bauers went 4-for-14 with a double, a home run and six RBI in the NLCS.

One of the best pure hitters in baseball, Díaz is batting .308/.341/.564 with four doubles, two home runs and four RBI this postseason out of the leadoff spot in the Tampa Bay lineup.

The 35-year-old led the AL in hits (180) during the regular season while posting a .293/.359/.446 line and 124 OPS+, and he has quietly put together a resume that ranks among the best in Tampa Bay franchise history.

Regular Season: 75 G, 4 SV, 15 HLD, 3.12 ERA, 116 K, 89.1 IP Postseason: 6 G, 2 SV, 1 HLD, 0.00 ERA, 11 K, 12.1 IP

Aaron Ashby is Milwaukee's leader in innings pitched this postseason, despite working exclusively in relief, and he has surrendered just four hits in 12.1 scoreless frames.

With one win, two saves and one hold, he has been the pitching staff's Swiss Army knife, filling a critical role akin to what Andrew Miller was for Cleveland during their 2016 World Series run.

Jacob Misiorowski is the unquestioned ace of the staff, Trevor Megill is an All-Star closer and Logan Henderson was one of the best pitchers in baseball during the second half of the season, but Ashby might be the single most important pitcher on the Brewers staff.

4. C William Contreras, Milwaukee Brewers

Regular Season: 147 G, .270/.341/.417, 46 XBH (18 HR), 94 RBI Postseason: 8 G, .367/.457/.700, 4 XBH (3 HR), 5 RBI

A three-time All-Star, two-time Silver Slugger winner and one of the best all-around catchers in baseball, William Contreras is the " straw that stirs the drink " for the Brewers.

He hits No. 3 in the Milwaukee lineup and had an .821 OPS with runners in scoring position this year, as he has proven time and again to have a knack for the big hit in the big moment. After going 5-for-14 with a double and a home run in the NLCS, he is swinging it as well as anyone for the Brewers.

His ability to control the running game (34.2% CS during regular season) will also be extremely important against a Rays team that tied for second in the majors with 164 steals.

Regular Season: 30 GS, 16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP Postseason: 3 GS, 2-0, 1.29 ERA, 0.76 WHIP, 23 K, 21.0 IP

Is there a more underrated pitcher in baseball right now than Drew Rasmussen?

The 31-year-old made his second straight All-Star team and is likely headed for a second straight top-10 finish in AL Cy Young balloting after ranking among the AL leaders in ERA (2.67, fourth), WHIP (0.91, first) and pitcher WAR (4.7, fourth).

He threw a gem against the Yankees in Game 1 of the ALDS (8.0 IP, 1 H, 0 ER, 10 K), and followed it up with a pair of quality starts in the ALCS. Nothing new for a pitcher who racked up 18 quality starts during the regular season.

For a Tampa Bay team that does a great job mixing and matching arms to get through games, he's the workhorse ace they can turn loose.

Regular Season: 162 G, .276/.360/.524, 68 XBH (42 HR), 101 RBI Postseason: 9 G, .273/.351/.455, 4 XBH (1 HR), 4 RBI

After breaking out with a 45-homer, 110-RBI season in 2025, Junior Caminero took his offensive game to another level this season, improving his walk rate and strikeout rate to log a 144 OPS+ and 5.7 WAR while again reaching the 40-homer mark.

Still only 23 years old and playing in his first postseason as an everyday player, Caminero is just scratching the surface of stardom, but no player on the Tampa Bay roster is capable of a bigger impact.

He went without a home run for the first eight games of the postseason, but went 2-for-4 with a long ball in the ALCS Game 6 clincher. That could be the perfect springboard to a huge World Series performance.

1. RHP Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers

Regular Season: 30 GS, 16-5, 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 252 K, 174.2 IP Postseason: 2 GS, 0-0, 3.24 ERA, 1.56 WHIP, 11 K, 8.1 IP

Jacob Misiorowski has made two starts this postseason, and neither has been particularly dominant.

NLDS Game 1: 4.0 IP, 4 H, 2 ER, 1 BB, 6 K NLCS Game 1: 4.1 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 3 BB, 5 K

However, he was the most dominant pitcher in baseball during the regular season, and with 11 days of rest since he last took the mound on Oct. 11 he should be fresh for his Game 1 start.

There is simply no starting pitcher who can match his high-octane stuff, and in a best-of-seven series, there is no more impactful player than the ace starter who could toe the rubber three times if the series goes the distance.

articles.title: 2026 World Series: How to watch Brewers and Rays after small ball carries them to Fall Classic
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays brought small ball back to baseball, ranking atop the league in batting average and sacrifice bunts.
articles.body: Chicks dig the ... small ball? Bunting, situational hitting, and productive outs had seemed to become a lost art in today's baseball. But the two teams in this year's World Series brought it all back. The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays were each the top seed in the National and American Leagues, respectively, and throughout this postseason, they've shown why. Now, one of those franchises will be crowned World Series champions for the first time, and all the action will be on FOX. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The Brewers had the second-lowest payroll in all of baseball, while the Rays had the eighth-smallest. Those payrolls have led to a heavy emphasis on analytics. But their analytics have zigged when the rest of the league's have zagged. It is no secret, despite how much people want to deny it, that home runs win (more on that later). That has been the case in the regular season as well as the postseason since stickball. Yet the Brewers and Rays ranked 29th and 22nd in total home runs this season. Their success, instead, has come at the hands of good old batting average - they both hit .258, good for the top two spots in the league. Both teams also had the highest batting averages with runners in scoring position (Rays were .284, Brewers were .276). Tampa Bay also ranked first in sacrifice bunts with 45, and Milwaukee's 37 were the fifth-most. That's not to say that bunting means you will win - the Los Angeles Dodgers had 23 combined sac bunts in 2024 and 2025, both seasons that ended in titles. But it works for the Rays and Brewers. The Rays (49) and Brewers (32) also ranked first and second in bunt hits. They also were tied for second in infield hits, behind only the Pittsburgh Pirates. In the days where exit velo has taken over (hitting the ball hard has always mattered, by the way), the Rays had the highest soft-hit percentage and second-worst hard-hit percentage. The Brewers ranked 12th and 18th in those categories and ranked sixth in medium-hit percentage. Nobody pulls the ball less often than the Brewers, and nobody goes up the middle and oppo more than they do, as well. The Brewers even hit ground balls at a higher rate than anybody and fly balls at the lowest (the Rays are fifth in grounders and 25th in fly balls). All of that is a tremendous shy-away from modern-day data taking over. Strikeouts have become more acceptable in baseball, but not in Florida. The Rays had the lowest strikeout percentage this season. Milwaukee, though, actually struck out at a higher percentage than most teams - they ranked 14th throughout the season, and they're actually striking out a ton this October. YANKEES OWNER HAL STEINBRENNER CONFIRMS HE SUPPORTS OWNERS' SALARY CAP PROPOSALS AHEAD OF LIKELY MLB LOCKOUT The Brewers have actually strayed away from their brand of baseball this October. In the National League Championship Series, they had the largest three-true-outcome percentage (home run, walk, strikeout) out of any LCS team since 1969. They were outhit in two games and struck out more than the Dodgers in each game. The walks shouldn't surprise anybody, as they had the highest walk rate in the regular season. But they out-homered the Dodgers in each game (the Dodgers went homerless in three of the games), and all season long, Milwaukee hit home runs that hurt badly. Despite hitting the second-fewest in the league, they actually had the ninth-most home runs with a runner on base and the highest percentage of multi-run homers in the league. The Rays also used the long ball throughout their American League Division Series against the New York Yankees and to clinch the pennant against the Cleveland Guardians. In all of this, the pitching cannot be dismissed. The Brewers have maybe the best pitcher in the sport in Jacob Misiorowski, and it feels like the Rays can pick up anyone reading this and turn them into a weapon on the bump. Brewers pitchers own a 2.03 ERA this postseason, while the Rays' staff sits at 2.59. Opponents are hitting just .183 and .201 off them, respectively, and they are allowing fewer than one homer per game. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Small ball and elite pitching undeniably got these small-market juggernauts to the big dance, but what they've proven this October is they can beat you in multiple ways - even by going the apparently dreaded "boom or bust." Now, all that is to be seen is which style while bring it home. All the action begins Friday in Milwaukee at 8 p.m. ET on FOX.

articles.title: Pros and Cons: Should the Mets sign Teruaki Sato?
articles.summary: Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato could be a strong Mets fit, with the team having a hole at first base.
articles.body:
The last time the Mets made a big splash by signing a position player from Japan was the only time they made a big splash signing a position player from Japan.

It was the 2003-04 offseason, and the player was Kaz Matsui , a power-hitting superstar infielder. The signing of Matsui was enormous at the time since it came on the heels of Ichiro Suzuki being the first-ever Japanese position player to be posted and signed by an MLB team -- in 2001 with the Mariners, when he won the MVP award. Shortly after Suzuki arrived, Hideki Matsui inked a deal with the Yankees during the 2002-03 offseason and made an immediate impact in the majors.

The Mets had signed a Japanese position player before, landing the flashy outfielder Tsuyoshi Shinjo ahead of the 2001 season. But Shinjo, while a fun player, was not viewed as a difference-maker.

Kaz Matsui was, though he didn't live up to the hype. He had a respectable .727 OPS in 2004 but flamed out quickly in New York, with a .670 OPS in 255 games over parts of three seasons before he was traded to Colorado in June of 2006. Matsui had some solid years for the Rockies and Astros later in his career, but never hit more than nine home runs in a season -- a massive disappointment after blasting 30-plus homers in back-to-back seasons for the Seibu Lions in Japan before coming to the majors.

Since Matsui, the Mets have been active in the Japanese market, but it has been limited to pitchers -- most recently the signing of Kodai Senga and strong pursuit of Yoshinobu Yamamoto before he landed with the Dodgers.

Meanwhile, Japanese position players have continued to wind up elsewhere.

Most recently, Shohei Ohtani went to the Angels and then the Dodgers (refusing to even consider an East Coast team), Seiya Suzuki signed with the Cubs, Kazuma Okamoto landed with the Blue Jays, and Munetaka Murakami inked a deal with the White Sox.

Another crop of Japanese stars is about to hit the open market this offseason, and slugging infielder Teruaki Sato could be a strong fit for New York.

Should the Mets pursue Sato? Here are the pros and cons...

Sato has reached another level offensively over the last two seasons for the Hanshin Tigers.

He smacked 40 homers and 34 doubles while posting a .924 OPS in 2025 as he won the Central League MVP award. Sato followed that up in 2026 with another monster season. In 143 games, he slashed .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs, 40 doubles, 100 runs scored, and 106 RBI -- winning the Triple Crown in the process.

Sato also excelled in a small sample against international competition in the 2026 World Baseball Classic, hitting .300/.417/.600 with three doubles in 12 plate appearances.

A look at Sato's advanced stats doesn't reveal any glaring issues. While he has a propensity to strike out (he fanned 164 times in 143 games in 2026), his strikeout percentage has been quite steady since 2023 -- and it actually ticked down a bit from 2025 (27.3 percent) to 2026 (26.7 percent) as his power output increased. Sato's BABIP in 2026 (.370) was a career high, so there should be some regression there. But his BABIP has always trended relatively high (.343 in 2024, .323 in 2025).

When it comes to durability, Sato has been a rock of sorts, appearing in 132 or more games in each of his first six seasons.

Sato also has youth on his side, as he'll be playing the entire 2027 season at just 28 years old.

While Sato has been primarily a third baseman and corner outfielder in Japan, many experts believe his defensive home in the majors will be at first base.

If Sato is indeed destined for first base, it would make him an ideal fit for a Mets team that still has a huge hole at the position. Jared Young performed admirably there this past season with Jorge Polanco injured and Mark Vientos ineffective, but Young -- who doesn't have much power and struggles against left-handed pitching -- might profile better in a reserve role.

While Sato might fit better at first base than third base, that doesn't mean he can definitely handle the position. At the same time, plenty of players have made a successful transition across the diamond, so there should be hope that a relatively athletic player like Sato can do it.

Another possible knock against Sato -- strictly when it comes to a possible Mets pursuit -- is that he hits from the left side of the plate.

The Mets are already very left-handed, with Juan Soto , Carson Benge , and A.J. Ewing among their key offensive cogs. But they do have some variety with the switch-hitting Francisco Lindor , both of their catchers ( Francisco Alvarez and Luis Torrens ), and Bo Bichette (if he opts in to his contract) all hitting from the right side.

As is noted above, Sato's strikeout rate for Hanshin in 2026 was 26.7 percent (164 K's in 143 games).

In 2024, in what was his last full season playing in Japan, Murakami's strikeout rate was 29.5 percent (180 in 143 games). In 69 games in 2025, Murakami's strikeout rate was 28.6 percent (71 in 69 games). In his first season for the White Sox, Murakami fanned a whopping 196 times in 127 games -- a rate of 35.4 percent.

Even though it's fair to expect Sato's strikeout rate to tick up as he transitions to the majors, there's no reason to believe it will be as stark as Murakami's increase.

In any event, even while striking out as often as he did in 2026, Murakami was still very valuable for Chicago, posting an .825 OPS (130 OPS+) and cracking 35 homers in 127 games.

With the Mets seemingly locked in at most positions on the diamond, the easiest way to move the needle offensively is to add someone to play first base or be the regular designated hitter. And with there being serious drawbacks to adding a DH-only player, the target should be first base.

There are other intriguing first basemen set to be on the free agent market, including Ty France . But none of them possess the upside of Sato.

Sato obviously comes with some risk, but it's time for the Mets to take a big swing on a high upside talent.

articles.title: 4 reasons to get excited about the World Series showdown between the Brewers and Rays
articles.summary: This introduction to the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will not make mention of which teams are not playing in the World Series – even if that’s all many folks want to talk about.
articles.body: This introduction to the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will not make mention of which teams are not playing in the World Series – even if that’s all many folks want to talk about. That would be a disservice to the very deserving teams that will take the field at 8 p.m. ET on Friday when the Brewers host the Rays in Game 1 of the Fall Classic. Suffice to say, however, that a neutral fan – and, given the size of the media markets directly involved, there are more of those than there have been in recent years – will likely have less of a visceral reaction to a Rays-Brewers World Series. If you are not from Milwaukee or the Tampa Bay area, perhaps you do not know who to root for or what to watch or, frankly, why to watch. Here are four reasons to tune in to this year’s edition: This is a clash of greatness – and familiarity Small payrolls may have imbued both teams with an underdog vibe as they made their way through the postseason bracket, but don’t be fooled: This matchup is total chalk, two one-seeds. The Tampa Bay Rays had the best record in the American League, the Brewers had the best record in the National League and all of Major League Baseball. That success is not entirely new, either. The Brewers had the best record in baseball last year, too, before they were swept out of the playoffs by the eventual champion Los Angeles Dodgers. In fact, if you go back to the start of 2024, the beginning of when that Dodger dominance started to feel inevitable, no team has won more games than the Milwaukee Brewers. The Rays, known for punching above their weight in the big-spending American League East, missed the playoffs entirely the past two years. But a longer lens reveals how they’ve earned a reputation as perennial contenders. The Rays, MLB’s newest team, made the playoffs for the first time in 2008. Starting with that season through today – a 19-year span – only the New York Yankees and Dodgers have won more regular season games. Within the sport, this sustained success has earned both organizations a reputation for being smart, savvy, and worth emulating. Front offices around the league are populated with people who honed their skills in Tampa or Milwaukee – and that actually includes Milwaukee. Matt Arnold, now the Brewers president of baseball operations, spent nearly a decade in the Rays’ organization before coming to Milwaukee. Just about 24 hours before the World Series began, Arnold greeted the current Rays’ president of baseball operations Erik Neander, who started as an intern in Tampa while Arnold was a scout there, on the field. Neander lifted Arnold airborne and wrapped him in a bear hug. “Still really good friends,” Arnold said of the relationships he still has in that front office. “Maybe not this week, but for sure for a lifetime. I consider them some of my closest friends.” Both teams are playing for the franchise’s first title All that respect and regular season success has yet to translate to a ring for either franchise. There are five MLB teams that have never won a World Series. After this season, there will be four. That alone imbues this series with compellingly straightforward stakes. For the Rays, it has been 29 years of existence and two failed trips to the Fall Classic, most recently in the neutral-site Covid-19 World Series in 2020. For the Brewers, it’s been 58 years of existence and they haven’t played in the final game of a season since 1982, before many of their current fans were even born. The Rays, in particular, are often mocked on a national level for their fickle Florida fanbase that would rather enjoy the year-round sun than sit in the necessary traffic to get to games in St. Petersburg. But when the broadcast cuts to either crowd in a clinching scenario, keep in mind the people who are there are hoping to see history made. Bring back batting average and balls in play and bunts Talk to your parents about baseball and see how quickly it takes them to bring up that, back in their day, hitters used to put the ball in play. Now, everyone just swings for the fences and all too often winds up striking out. Well, mom and dad, have I got good news for you. Tune in to this World Series for a throwback in style. The matchup features the two teams with the highest batting averages in the regular season – the Brewers were best in the sport, the Rays a close second. The Rays had the lowest strikeout rate in the game. The Brewers scored the second-most runs in the sport while hitting the second fewest home runs. You will probably see someone bunt for a hit. The Rays’ 49 bunt hits in the regular season were not only a league-high this season, it’s the most any team has had since 2008. The Brewers were second in the sport this season in bunt hits. And if it’s Rays’ speed specialist Chandler Simpson who reaches first on a ball that fails to leave the infield, you will probably see a stolen base soon after. Simpson’s 46 steals led the American League in the regular season. He has never hit a home run in the majors. This style tends to amount to close, low-scoring games. So maybe not the most fireworks, but plenty of drama. There’s still plenty of power and pop Something else you’re likely to see in this World Series? The fastest pitch and the slowest home run trot in Fall Classic history. The former will undoubtedly be supplied by Jacob Misiorowski, the Brewers’ 24-year-old flame-throwing phenom and probable Cy Young Award winner. To set a new speed record, he needs to top the 103.2 mph reached by Aroldis Chapman in 2016. And will he? Oh, absolutely. His first pitch of the Brewers’ postseason this year was 104.8 mph. The Miz is a miracle of mechanics and strength and human extremes. “Arguably one of the best arms to ever touch a dirt circle in the big leagues,” Kyle Snyder, the opposing Rays pitching coach, told CNN Sports. “I mean, what a fantastic season and what an incredible talent.” That blink-and-you’ll-miss-it stuff will be juxtaposed on the basepaths by the unhurried one-man parade put on by Rays’ third baseman Junior Caminero if he homers. And will he? He’s got as good a chance as anyone else who steps to the plate this series. Over the past two seasons combined, Caminero has the second-most home runs in baseball. He’s 23 years old, playing in his first postseason, and soaking up every second of it. When he homered in the clinch Game 6 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians, Caminero staged an elaborate celebration that took 38.66 seconds to round the base paths. It was the slowest uninterrupted playoff home trot since MLB Statcast started measuring in 2015 – and the second slowest ever, behind only another one from Caminero in September of this season. The Miz and Junior aren’t yet household names. But this World Series could change that.

articles.title: Rays, Brewers Unveil 2026 MLB World Series Rosters Ahead of Historic Showdown
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers announced their 2026 World Series rosters on Friday.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers announced their 2026 World Series rosters on Friday.

The most notable change from the teams' American League Championship Series and National League Championship Series rosters is the Brewers' addition of pitcher Brandon Woodruff.

Per MLB.com's Adam McCalvy , Woodruff was seemingly headed for season-ending surgery after leaving a July start with an injury to his throwing shoulder, but when scans showed improvement in August, he decided to start a throwing program in hopes of being a factor in the playoffs.

While Woodruff was not fully healed in time for the National League Division Series or NLCS, he is on the roster and could be a factor for the Brew Crew in their first World Series appearance since 1982.

The Rays and Brewers will clash in Game 1 of the 2026 Fall Classic on Friday night at American Family Field in Milwaukee.

McCalvy noted that someone with knowledge of the situation called it "50-50" regarding whether Woodruff would make the Brewers' roster, but now that he has, the focus shifts toward how he will be deployed.

It may be too much to ask for Woodruff to start a game in the World Series after being out for over three months, so he may be best utilized as a bullpen option.

However, Woodruff has not pitched out of the bullpen since his second MLB season in 2018.

A Brewer for his entire career, Woodruff is a two-time All-Star with a career record of 55-30 to go along with a 3.10 ERA and 918 strikeouts over 790.1 innings.

Injuries have limited him to 21 starts combined over the past three seasons, but Woodruff has long been an impactful, ace-level starter for the Brew Crew when healthy.

The Brewers' unquestioned current ace and NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski is getting the start in Game 1 against Nick Martinez.

Manager Pat Murphy's plans beyond that remain to be seen, although Logan Henderson seems most likely to start Game 2, while Dustin May, Robert Gasser and possibly even Woodruff are in the mix after that.

The Rays' World Series roster is largely the same as their ALCS squad with the exception of reliever Garrett Cleavinger, who replaces Brody Hopkins.

Cleavinger, a lefty, struggled during the regular season to the tune of a 4.79 ERA, but he was one of Tampa's most important relievers last season, posting a 2.35 ERA over 67 appearances.

Of course, both teams will lean heavily on their star players, headlined by third baseman Junior Caminero and starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen for the Rays, and Misiorowski and outfielder Jackson Chourio for the Brewers.

The winner of the 2026 World Series will go down in history since both the Rays and Brewers are searching for their first-ever World Series title.

articles.title: LA Times sportswriter has unhinged Shohei Ohtani take after Dodgers fall short of World Series
articles.summary: After the Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers, an LA Times sports columnist wrote that Shohei Ohtani should stop pitching or the Dodgers should trade him.
articles.body: Well, this might be the most insane piece of "advice" you'll ever hear directed at a Major League Baseball team. The Los Angeles Dodgers failed to reach the World Series for the third consecutive season, getting swept by the unrelenting Milwaukee Brewers superteam. For most Dodgers fans, it was disappointing, sure, but the success of the previous two years, the big postseason moments from superstar players, and the parades through Los Angeles dampened the blow relative to other seasons. But local sports media have spent the past week searching for the explanation for LA's "failure." The actual reason the Dodgers lost, that the postseason in baseball is little more than a coin flip and small sample sizes flatten out any talent advantage, is boring and uninteresting. For example, in game four, the Brewers' expected batting average was .237, while LA's was .296. Milwaukee scored six runs, though the Dodgers scored just four – which is how we get to this week's article from Bill Plaschke at the Los Angeles Times. BREWERS OFFICIALLY END DODGERS DYNASTY WITH RIDICULOUS 6-4 COMEBACK IN GAME FOUR TO COMPLETE NLCS SWEEP His postmortem of the Dodgers' season places much of the blame on, uh, Shohei Ohtani. There's a kernel of truth to it; Ohtani was clearly limited by several injuries down the stretch, with a lengthy slump accompanying an increase in chase rate and swing and miss. There's no way to tell how those injuries happened. Yes, Ohtani had returned to pitching full time in 2026, but LA's famously careful with Ohtani on the mound, and there's no indication that it was directly responsible for him getting hurt. But the whole team struggled offensively in October, with a .195/.267/.323 batting line and a remarkable .116 batting average with runners in scoring position. Going 5-43 with runners in scoring position isn't going to cut it, and it's a far bigger problem than just one player. The big debate though, that Plaschke references, is whether Ohtani should continue pitching, being a two-way player, in 2027 and beyond. Ohtani and the team have already said he intends to do both next year, but Plashcke believes he knows better. "...He's changing. His body is changing. His skills are changing. He's 32, with 13 seasons of professional baseball burdening his lumbering 6-foot-4 frame, and part of his game is slowly disintegrating under the weight." "Lumbering" is an odd way to describe a player who stole 50 bases two seasons ago, but don't worry, it gets worse. "The problem is his pitching," Plaschke continues, saying that it's "distracting him" and "exhausting him" and that "enough is enough." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE That's debatable, sure, but again, there's logic to it. Ohtani is such a valuable hitter that there's a case to be made for him to focus exclusively on being a DH. But what he says next has well, no logic or reason behind it whatsoever. "They need to pull him off the pitching mound permanently. And if he insists on continuing this detrimental charade, they need to seriously consider trading him." Alright, well now we've officially left the world of rationality and gone into some sort of bizarre performance art trolling act. Or something. Hopefully. Trading Shohei Ohtani is somewhere beyond insane. Even if he hurt his arm and required surgery to miss nine months and permanently put pitching behind him, trading him would be insane. Even if he only pitches 50-70 innings a year, that's immensely valuable combined with his hitting prowess. For context, top end relievers are making $20+ million a season to throw 60-70 innings. Ohtani's offense is worth $50-60 million a year, and even in limited usage, his pitching is worth at least the additional $20 million if not much more. With the upside of even greater value. Then there's the fact that with Ohtani pitching in 2025, the Dodgers won the World Series. Including game three, when Ohtani hit two homers to help get the game to extra innings. Then there was game four of the 2025 NLCS, when he had arguably the single greatest performance in baseball history. Going six shutout innings with 10 strikeouts and hitting three home runs, including one that literally left Dodger Stadium. But that's the baseball side of it. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Ohtani is such a transcendent star that he's worth hundreds of millions of dollars a year to Los Angeles in advertising, marketing, and promotions. His contract, even at a heavily deferred $70 million per season, is one of the biggest bargains in the sport. The extra revenue he brings in has allowed the Dodgers to go from being a top three or four spending team to being number one. The rush from the other 29 teams to acquire him would be quite literally hilarious, because trading Ohtani would be an act of financial suicide for LA and a massive windfall for a new team. Plashcke is frequently not a serious person, but this is enough to warrant serious questioning of his ability to continue writing about baseball for a "legitimate" newspaper. The LA Times should ask him to focus on his one true love; left-wing politics. Clearly, his attempt to try to do both is hurting both himself, and the paper, and should lead to some very serious conversations between the two sides.

articles.summary: After missing on a Paul Skenes Opening Day bet, a postseason pick backs Jacob Misiorowski and the Milwaukee Brewers over the Tampa Bay Rays.
articles.body: It feels like just yesterday that I was betting on Paul Skenes to light up the Mets and keep them from scoring on Opening Day of the baseball season. articles.title: 1 MLB Player Is Guaranteed to Receive a World Series Ring Regardless of Rays vs. Brewers Result
articles.summary: Congratulations are in order for 2026 World Series champion Jake Woodford.
articles.body:
Congratulations are in order for 2026 World Series champion Jake Woodford.

Even though Game 1 of the Fall Classic between the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers has yet to be played, MLB revealed that Woodford is guaranteed to receive a ring no matter what having spent time with both clubs this season.

Woodford, a right-handed relief pitcher, is currently with the Rays after signing a minor-league deal in August. He started this season with Milwaukee, appearing in 16 games out of the bullpen, then was released in July.

After a brief stint with the Chicago Cubs, Woodford joined the Rays as part of their Triple-A club. He was called up on Sept. 24 and made his lone regular-season appearance with Tampa that same day.

Woodford is no longer on the Rays' 26-man roster after being designated for assignment after that Sept. 24 appearance, so he won't play in the Fall Classic.

Still, a guarantee to be recognized as a member of the 2026 World Series champion is a nice consolation prize for a journeyman reliever.

Woodford has spent time in eight different organizations since being drafted by the St. Louis Cardinals in 2015. He made his MLB debut with the Cardinals in 2020.

The 29-year-old has pitched in 130 MLB games with seven different teams. He owns a 5.36 ERA in 283.2 innings.

articles.title: Will The World Series Come Down To An ABS Challenge? It’s Possible.
articles.summary: By itself, the World Series should be spectacular. Add in ABS, and it should be mesmerizing. Here's why:
articles.body:
With the World Series beginning tonight, all eyes are on baseball. While the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays have certainly had impressive seasons, the real star of the game has been the rookie Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) Challenge System that's used to help mediate balls and strikes. It operates on a secure network developed by Major League Baseball (MLB) with T-Mobile . Most fans love it, as do the players I've spoken to about it.

It's officially transformed baseball from a game of potential human error into a high-stakes, high-tech game of poker. The numbers tell a fascinating story about who holds the cards, when they bluff, and how October baseball has turned up the volume on digital appeals.

During the regular season, according to MLB, the ABS quietly established its rhythm. Teams challenged an average of 4.4 pitches per game, or roughly 2.2 challenges per team, with human eyes proving far from perfect as players walked away with a 53.9% overturn rate. By the playoffs, the safety net shrank and the stakes skyrocketed. Through the end of the National and American League Championship Series, challenge usage climbed slightly to 4.6 pitches per game, and accuracy surged to a 60.5% overturn rate. When every single pitch can define a season, players stop guessing and start calling out genuine mistakes with surgical precision.

But players aren't challenging the first pitch they dislike. The ABS challenge is a limited resource, and teams covet it like gold. Early on in games, from the 1st through the 3rd innings, players initiated only 28.6% of all challenges as managers and players hoarded their two allotted appeals. By the 7th inning and beyond, those stored challenges came out of the vault to account for 39.1% of all reviews.

The raw volume of challenges across different counts can be equally deceiving. The majority of regular-season challenges, 59.6% occurred in 0-0 counts, which sounds high until you realize 0-0 is the most frequent count in baseball. In reality, players challenged a tiny 2% of all 0-0 pitches. The true battles occurred on edge-case counts where a single call alters an entire at-bat. On 3-2 counts, players challenged 9.3% of all pitches, representing the highest challenge rate of any count. More broadly, 6.2% of all three-ball pitches were challenged compared to 4% of two-strike pitches. A missed call on 0-0 is an annoyance, but a missed call on a full count is the difference between a game-changing walk and an inning-ending strikeout.

Comparing how tonight's teams navigated the system reveals starkly different strategies. The Brewers adopted an aggressive, fire-at-will approach. After averaging 2.4 challenges per game in the regular season (8th most in MLB) with a 52.8% overturn rate, Milwaukee ramped up to 3.4 challenges per game in the postseason so far while improving its success rate to 59.2%. The Brewers used the system as an offensive weapon, putting relentless pressure on the opposition.

The Rays went in the opposite direction. After averaging 2.1 challenges per game in the regular season (13th in MLB) with a matching 52.8% overturn rate, they dialed back to a disciplined 1.4 challenges per game in the playoffs. Their reward for extreme restraint was a staggering 69% overturn rate. They rarely challenged, but when they did, the robo-ump almost always agreed.

Interestingly, during the regular season, catchers initiated 53% of all challenges, batters accounted for 45%, and pitchers managed 2%. Pitchers, watching from 60 feet and 6 inches away through a wall of bodies, simply lack the visual angle to contest borderline pitch locations. Brewers star pitcher Jacob Misiorowski told me this summer that he completely trusts his catcher to challenge, and I feel most pitchers agree. And with good reason: In the postseason, catchers have cemented their status as masters of the strike zone by initiating 61% of all challenges, while batter usage dropped to 39% and pitchers initiated just one challenge. Equipped with a squatted view right behind the glove, modern catchers are no longer just framing pitches but acting as real-time judges, deciding in a fraction of a second whether to trust the umpire's call or overrule it with a flick of their wrist.

ABS has added incredible drama to games. And I expect in the World Series, the timeliness and importance of each call may be crucial to which team will win its first-ever Fall Classic title.
